newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Short-end of core Europe offers haven.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Short-end of core Europe offers haven.

text.p: Bond investors fleeing peripheral Europe should look to the short end of core markets for the most defensive positioning, analysts said on Wednesday.
The safe-haven appeal of core French and German debt assets is enhanced at the short end of the yield curve by the prospect of immediate returns, as well as currency protection, they said.

"There is a desire for defensive trades on both sides of the Atlantic, and if you are an investor who wants to stay in the market, then go shorter in duration," said Sonia Gibbs, senior market strategist at Nomura International in London.
Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London said as the year progresses, the short end of core Europe will perform well.
"The Bundesbank is content to keep monetary policy on hold, but they will be forced to ease in the second quarter as signs of economic weakness come through," he said.
But he said France was less attractive, although interest rates should fall below those in Germany. The French intervention rate is at 3.10 percent, while the German repo rate is 3.0 percent.
"It's clear that the Bank of France is being very cautious," he said. "If we continue to see talk of EMU delay that will underpin the mark, and the French short end will underperform."
Gibbs also said any sign of EMU delay was likely to be mark supportive, as it would assuage fears that the new euro currency would not go ahead in 1999 in a form weaker than the mark.

"If you feel the dollar has some downside potential,then that adds to the short end as a defensive play," she said. "The safe-haven appeal will also have potential currency gains in France and Germany."
Other analysts favoured moving down the curve as a defence against the threat of a sell-off in the bond markets.
Andy Bevan, senior international bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London, said such a sell-off would have less impact at the short end than on the longer durations.
"We'd move to the short end as a purely defensive action," said "We want to be out of the long end, coming shorter to cash because we don't like bonds."
Bevan said he was fighting shy of the Danish bond market.
"Policy gears in Denmark are inappropriately set," he said. "Growth is barrelling along and the soft mark is stopping them from tightening policy."
Gibbs advised steering clear of the Netherlands, as there was a chance the special advances rate could be raised as soon as Thursday. The rate is currently at 2.5 percent.
"Even if they don't raise tomorrow, growth is strong and that makes the short end risky," she said.
The short end of the U.S. was also ruled out, as the likelihood of a rate rise was "too close to call", analysts said.

Stamenkovic said the U.S. short end was the most risky of debt markets, as the Federal Reserve was content with the state of the economy, but concerned about the labour market. He was not expecting an imminent hike in U.S. interest rates.
Gibbs said the outlook for U.S. Treasuries would improve once the market gets over the hurdle of the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan later on Wednesday.
Bevan said he was expecting to see investors heading to the shorter end of the market anytime soon, but so far there was little evidence that this was the case.
"We are not yet seeing a significant breakdown at the longer end," said Bevan. "What we'd like to see before we pull the trigger is a sign that sentiment is turning against the core markets."
